routes.n: Tashkent: Bek Broker and the Triple Seven cargo (2023)
routes.what: RFE/RL's Systema unit reported on 6 Sep 2024 that artworks unloaded from the yacht Triple Seven at Vlissingen by the Dutch shipper Kortmann Art Packers and Shippers B.V. in early January 2023 went from Amsterdam airport to Tashkent and on to Moscow, reaching Aleksei Repik, a pharmaceutical magnate sanctioned by Britain in February 2023, three days after leaving Tashkent. Bek Broker, a Tashkent firm with a Moscow affiliate, handled the Uzbek and Russian legs. The cargo was 44 items worth US$4.6m, including works by Dalí, Renoir and Matisse; Nawton Ltd, a BVI company managing the yacht, paid the shipper. A second shipment of about US$286,000 went to Tashkent in February 2023 on a customs document signed by Alla Okroyan, wife of Mkrtich Okroyan, sanctioned by the US in September 2023. Customs data showed Bek Broker made 8,700 shipments from Russia to Uzbekistan and 106 the other way in 2018–2022, then 1,962 shipments into Russia after the invasion worth US$41.6m, of which art was US$36.6m. The control at issue was the March 2022 EU, US and Swiss luxury-goods ban covering art above €300. Kortmann said it did not know the final destination; Polina Repik said the art went to an unnamed museum; British lawyer Alex Prezanti said a shipper's liability turns on what it knew or should have known.
src: RFE/RL (Systema), 'For Some Russian Art Collectors, Uzbekistan Is How You Avoid Sanctions', 6 Sep 2024

routes.n: London 2022: the Western houses close the Russian sale
routes.what: On 15 March 2022 Sotheby's and Christie's cancelled their June 2022 London Russian art sales within hours of each other; Bonhams cancelled its 15 June sale the next day. Phillips, Russian-owned, kept selling and gave £5.8m from an evening sale to the Ukrainian Red Cross. Sotheby's November 2021 Russian Week had totalled £17.7m with fees, more than all other houses' Russian sales combined; the June sales had been popular with London-based Russians and regional collectors in Russia, among them Rustam Aliev, a Kaliningrad dairy tycoon who bought Bulatov and Vassiliev works for £189,000 and £220,500 in December 2021. The same day the UK, with its G7 allies, announced a ban on exports of high-end luxury goods, including art and antiques, to Russia; Rishi Sunak, Chancellor of the Exchequer, framed it as economic pressure. Selling art to a Russian individual stayed legal; dealing with a designated person did not. By 2024 Polina Sokolova, antiques and art expert at the Russian Auction House (RAD), told Izvestia that the major British houses barred anyone linked to Russia, dual nationals included, and that proxy buying was not worth it because EU exports of luxury goods above €300 to Russia were prohibited. Christie's and Sotheby's also closed their Moscow offices after the invasion.

routes.n: Dubai: where Moscow's money and galleries went (2022–2024)
routes.what: The Art Newspaper reported on 18 January 2023 that wealthy Russians had flocked to the UAE: the share of private jets flying from Russia to the UAE rose from 3% to 14% between March and June 2022; Christie's added a Russian-speaking staff member, formerly of the Tretyakov Gallery, to its Dubai office; Tatintsian Gallery became the first Russian gallery in Alserkal Avenue while its Moscow venue closed indefinitely; Dubai gallerist Natalya Andakulova said Russian 'relocants' wanting to decorate their homes had become her main audience; Benedetta Ghione, executive director of Art Dubai, described an influx of wealthy international collectors; Vera Alkhova, who runs a Russian-language Telegram channel on the Gulf art scene, said 'half of Moscow is in Dubai'. The Art Basel and UBS survey noted additional trade in luxury objects and artworks between Russia and the Gulf states or Turkey driven by Western restrictions. Christie's said all Dubai clients undergo anti-money-laundering and sanctions due diligence. The customs mirror agrees with the press: the UAE declared US$11.64m of works of art imported from Russia in 2024, almost all paintings, the largest Russian art arc in any opened partner data, and US$65m of chapter 71 exports to Russia, including US$20.7m of jewellery and US$18.6m of diamonds.

routes.n: Yerevan: the re-export economy and its art line (2022–2024)
routes.what: bne IntelliNews (19 Sep 2024, Seymur Mammadov, Baku) set out the Armenian pattern from National Statistical Committee data: exports to Russia tripled in 2022 to US$2.4bn and reached a record US$3.4bn in 2023; Russia's share of Armenian exports went from 27% to 40–44%; goods Armenia does not make, such as phones (US$499m), cars (US$378m) and monitors (US$250m), led the list, and 'art and collectibles' was among the categories whose exports to Russia multiplied (19 times, base not stated). Gold exports under Armenian origin reached US$1.8bn in 2023 and US$2.5bn in the first months of 2024; diamonds US$589m in 2023. The control that bit was the EU's diamond regime: a ban on direct imports of non-industrial diamonds and diamond jewellery from Russia from January 2024, a partial embargo on Russian stones processed in third countries from 1 March and a full one from 1 September 2024. Alexey Overchuk, First Deputy Chairman of the Russian Government, forecast 2024 turnover of US$14–16bn. In the art statistics the Armenian leg is small: the EU declared US$0.77m of art imported from Armenia in 2025, Hong Kong US$10.7k in 2024; the Armenia–Russia HS 97 rows were not opened.

routes.n: Almaty, Tashkent, Tbilisi: new collector bases, old gold corridor
routes.what: Jo Vickery, writing in Art Focus Now on 1 December 2025, named Georgia, Uzbekistan and Kazakhstan as places with growing collector bases for Russian non-conformist art, while the market for it 'blossoms' in Moscow and Russian diaspora buyers abroad favour Imperial and academic works. The customs picture for Central Asia is metal, not canvas: Kazakhstan declared US$188.2m of chapter 71 exports to Russia in 2024, of which gold was US$178.4m and jewellery US$4.5m; works of art do not appear among its top 24 export categories to Russia (total US$9.55bn). Vedomosti (8 Apr 2025) reported that after 2022 European galleries at Moscow fairs were largely replaced by galleries from Asia and the Middle East, and that Cosmoscow's attendance rose more than fivefold since 2020 to about 50,000. The Kazakhstan–Russia and Uzbekistan–Russia HS 97 rows were not opened; the only quantified Uzbek art line is the Bek Broker customs record above (US$36.6m of art declared into Russia after February 2022).

routes.n: London after 2022: Fabergé and the Imperial market without Russia
routes.what: Russian-origin art still enters Britain: HMRC-based Comtrade data show US$6.05m of chapter 97 imports from Russia in 2025, half of it antiques. The selling side has reorganised around diaspora and international buyers. On 2 December 2025 Christie's London sold the Fabergé Winter Egg (1913, by Alma Theresia Pihl) for £22.9m, a record for any Fabergé object against the £8.9m Rothschild egg of 2007; The Art Newspaper (Anny Shaw, 3 Dec 2025) did not identify seller or buyer. Sotheby's 'Fabergé, Imperial & Revolutionary Art' sale the same week was, per Art Focus Now, the first Russian sale since 2022 in all but name; Aivazovsky's 'The Survivors' made over US$5m, and the paintings auction sold all but two lots for US$1.5m; MacDougall's ran an online 'From Icons to Non-Conformists' sale with six Rabin paintings at around €25,000 each. Buyers bid online, by phone and in the room; diaspora collectors favour Imperial art, international ones modern and contemporary. US enforcement reached London too: Graham Bonham-Carter, a UK businessman, was indicted in October 2022 for trying to ship more than a dozen of Oleg Deripaska's artworks from the US to London in 2021 after an auction house said it believed the works were Deripaska's.

routes.n: Enforcement: from the Rotenberg report to the New York subpoenas (2020–2023)
routes.what: The US Senate Permanent Subcommittee on Investigations (Sens. Rob Portman and Tom Carper) reported on 29 July 2020 that Gregory Baltser, a Moscow-based art adviser who founded the BALTZER agency in 2013, bought over US$18m of art between May and November 2014 with funds traced to shell companies linked to Arkady and Boris Rotenberg, sanctioned on 20 March 2014; Rotenberg-linked companies moved at least US$91m through the US financial system after the sanctions; Magritte's 'La Poitrine' was bought privately for US$7.5m with Highland Ventures taking title and Advantage Alliance wiring the funds; Sotheby's, Christie's, Phillips and Bonhams had not asked Baltser for whom he bought. The report asked Congress to extend the Bank Secrecy Act to high-value art, as the EU does above €10,000, and OFAC to narrow the IEEPA 'artworks' exception. After February 2022 the controls were used: Britain seized a Fabergé egg of Viktor Vekselberg in May 2022; German police took 30 paintings and four Fabergé eggs from Alisher Usmanov's yacht in November 2022; in February 2023 federal prosecutors in New York subpoenaed several auction houses for years of sales records concerning Andrey Melnichenko, Viktor Vekselberg, Roman Abramovich and Ihor Kolomoisky. Sotheby's said it operates in strict compliance with global sanctions.
src: US Senate PSI, Portman–Carper press release, 29 Jul 2020
The Art Newspaper, 'US authorities subpoena auction houses', 7 Feb 2023

routes.n: Moscow turns inward: the domestic auction boom (2023–2025)
routes.what: With the London sales gone and the luxury-goods bans in force, Russian collectors bought at home. ARTinvestment.RU's Egor Molchanov told Izvestia (29 Mar 2024) that Russian auction turnover rose more than 125% in 2023 to above US$25m, the best result in 13 years, and that collectors had returned from Europe to the domestic market and Russian artists. Litfund doubled its auctions to 120 a year over three years with turnover growth of 20–25% a year and a record February 2024; Sergei Podstannitsky of the Auction Holding said turnover had not fallen and high-price sales were rising; the Russian Auction House said no pieces were arriving from European auctions and demand exceeded supply. Bidspirit's Alexander Kiselevsky put the 2024 market at about 10.3bn roubles with Moscow about 70% (Vedomosti, 8 Apr 2025). Prices followed: Shishkin's 'Girl in a pine forest' (1889) made 85m roubles at the Moscow Auction House in June 2024 and Vasnetsov's 'Pilgrims' 135m roubles in March 2025. Vladey's 28 November 2024 sale exceeded €900,000, with Oleg Tselkov's 'Child with a balloon' (1988) at €575,000 bought by the musician and collector Timati (RBC Style, 6 Dec 2024).
src: Izvestia, 'Торги уместны: аукционный рынок России вырос вдвое', 29 Mar 2024
RBC Style, Vladey sale report, 6 Dec 2024

routes.n: Istanbul: a transit for people and works, not a declared cargo lane
routes.what: Delovoy Peterburg (Alexander Tupeko, 23 Nov 2024) quoted the St Petersburg graphic artist Alexander Ionov-Lesh on how Russian contemporary work now reaches Europe: 'you take the works and fly to Europe via Istanbul'; he exhibited in Sweden in 2022 and called logistics the main problem. The same piece reported that Russian museums cannot ship originals abroad and stage photo exhibitions instead, that Eastern institutions have replaced European partners (Hermitage shows in Oman in 2025; Russian Museum avant-garde in China in 2024), and quoted Mikhail Shvydkoy, presidential special envoy for international cultural cooperation (May 2024), on continuing demand for Russian heritage. The customs record matches a hand-carry corridor rather than a freight one: Russia declared US$10,308 of chapter 97 exports to Turkey in 2021 and US$10,925 of imports from Turkey in 2020; Turkey's chapter 97 exports to the whole world in 2023 were under US$0.3m across 9705–9706; works of art appear in neither direction's top 24 categories on Trading Economics for 2025, when Turkey sold Russia US$6.73bn of goods and bought US$42.37bn. The Turkey–Russia HS 97 pages for 2022–2025 exist on Trading Economics but were not opened, so a post-2022 figure is not given.

routes.n: Hong Kong and China: gold moves, art does not
routes.what: Hong Kong's 2025 customs return shows what the Moscow–Hong Kong arc is made of: US$13.01bn of pearls, precious stones, metals and coins out of US$13.12bn of total imports from Russia, against US$199,680 of works of art and US$819,180 of clocks and watches. The China–Russia HS 97 pages were not opened. Press evidence for Russian buying in Hong Kong salerooms was not found in the opened sources; the Izvestia piece (29 Mar 2024) carried the auction house 12-й Стул's view that the British houses' block signalled to buyers from China, Asia and the Middle East that their purchases might face similar limits, and Vedomosti (8 Apr 2025) recorded Asian galleries replacing European ones at Moscow fairs. moscow.dossier: Moscow is the one art capital whose outbound arcs the customs record barely shows and whose inbound arcs it cannot show at all, because the Federal Customs Service stopped publishing detailed trade data in 2022. What is known comes from partners and the press. Before the war the declared art corridors were Western: Russia recorded US$21.35m of works of art imported from Switzerland in 2021, almost all antiques, and only US$10,308 of art exported to Turkey. On 15 March 2022 Sotheby's and Christie's cancelled their June London Russian sales and Bonhams followed; the same day the UK and its G7 allies announced the luxury-goods export ban that put chapter 97 above €300 (EU) and the whole of chapter 97 (UK Schedule 3A, 14 April 2022) off limits for Russia. Christie's and Sotheby's closed their Moscow offices. The money went to Dubai: The Art Newspaper (18 Jan 2023) recorded Christie's Russian-speaking hire there, Tatintsian Gallery's move to Alserkal Avenue and Russian relocants as a Dubai gallerist's main audience, and the UAE declared US$11.64m of art imported from Russia in 2024, the largest Russian art arc in any opened partner data. The freight went through Tashkent: RFE/RL's Systema (6 Sep 2024) traced US$4.6m of art from the yacht Triple Seven via Amsterdam and Tashkent to Aleksei Repik in Moscow in January 2023, and a Tashkent broker's US$36.6m of declared art shipments into Russia after the invasion. Yerevan became a re-export hub for gold, diamonds and electronics (exports to Russia US$3.4bn in 2023, bne IntelliNews 19 Sep 2024), with art and collectibles a small multiplied line. Istanbul is where artists and works change planes (Delovoy Peterburg, 23 Nov 2024), not a declared cargo lane. At home the market turned inward and grew: auction turnover up more than 125% in 2023 to above US$25m (ARTinvestment.RU, Izvestia 29 Mar 2024), about 10.3bn roubles in 2024 with Moscow 70% (Bidspirit, Vedomosti 8 Apr 2025); the houses are Litfund (120 sales a year), Vladey (weekly online sales from €100; €900,000 on 28 Nov 2024), the Auction Holding's Moscow Auction House (Shishkin at 85m roubles, June 2024), the Russian Auction House, ArtInvestment's 'Первые имена', Russkaya Emal, V Nikitskom and Antikvarium; the fairs are Cosmoscow (about 50,000 visitors), ART Moscow, the Russian Antiques Salon and blazar, with Asian and Middle Eastern galleries in the stands the Europeans left. London still takes Russian-origin art (US$6.05m declared in 2025) and sold the Fabergé Winter Egg for £22.9m on 2 December 2025, but the Russian-resident bidder is gone from its rooms.

houses.scale: About 120 auctions a year by 2024, double the count of three years earlier; turnover growth 20–25% a year; record February 2024 (+30–35%). Books, manuscripts and art: a first edition of 'Eugene Onegin' made 26m roubles in 2023 (estimate 12m). Sergei Burmistrov, CEO, estimated Moscow's 2024 market at 7–7.5bn roubles and said new buyers use art as an investment.

Contemporary and modern Russian art; weekly online sales starting from €100 and live evening sales. The 28 November 2024 sale exceeded €900,000 across 62 lots, about half sold; top lot Oleg Tselkov, 'Child with a balloon' (1988), €575,000 (65m roubles), bought by the musician and collector Timati. Founder and head Vladimir Ovcharenko.

houses.scale: Classical Russian painting and graphics. Shishkin, 'Girl in a pine forest' (1889), 85m roubles in June 2024 at the Moscow Auction House, cited as a record; Konchalovsky from the Gromyko collection 7.5m roubles (2024). Co-founders Sergei Podstannitsky (Izvestia, 2024) and Alexander Popov (Vedomosti, 2025).

Market data provider and auction platform; head Egor Molchanov is the source of the 2023 turnover figure (more than 125% growth, above US$25m). Its 'Первые имена' sale offered an Aivazovsky landscape with a 73.6m-rouble reserve (March 2024).
Online auction aggregator used by Russian houses; its head Alexander Kiselevsky put the 2024 Russian art market at about 10.3bn roubles, Moscow about 70%.

houses.n: Fairs: Cosmoscow, ART Moscow, Russian Antiques Salon, blazar
houses.scale: Cosmoscow's visitors rose more than fivefold since 2020 to about 50,000; founder Margarita Pushkina. ART Moscow and the Russian Antiques Salon are run by Expo-Park (CEO Vasily Bychkov). After 2022 European galleries were largely replaced by galleries from Asia and the Middle East. Cosmoscow had earlier cited ties to Qatar and plans for Dubai (The Art Newspaper, 18 Jan 2023). Gallery results at Cosmoscow 2024: Kosolapov 7.4m roubles (Syntax), Chernysheva 4m roubles (Iragui).

walls.n: EU: luxury-goods export ban covering works of art, collectors' pieces and antiques above €300
walls.cite: Council Regulation (EU) 2022/428 of 15 March 2022 amending Regulation (EU) No 833/2014, inserting Article 3h ('3 nonies') and Annex XVIII; heading 9700 listed among luxury goods; prohibition on sale, supply, transfer or export of listed items above €300 per item to Russia or for use in Russia; jewellery, silverware, tapestries and clocks also listed, musical instruments above €1,500, vehicles above €50,000.
walls.authority: Council of the European Union; applied in France by the Ministère de la Culture, which suspended export authorisations (Cerfa 02-0076, 02-0083, EU licence 11033*03) for goods bound for Russia or for listed Russian nationals and warned that customs will block such goods at the border even with a valid authorisation, save exemptions such as diplomatic missions under Article 3h(3).
src: Ministère de la Culture (France), 'Avertissement: le régime de circulation des biens culturels est concerné par les sanctions européennes', 6 Apr 2022

walls.n: UK: Schedule 3A luxury goods — the whole of chapter 97, no price floor
walls.cite: Russia (Sanctions) (EU Exit) Regulations 2019 (S.I. 2019/855), Schedule 3A (Luxury goods), inserted at 5 p.m. on 14 April 2022 by the Russia (Sanctions) (EU Exit) (Amendment) (No. 8) Regulations 2022 (S.I. 2022/452). Paragraph 21: 'Works of art, collectors' pieces and antiques, meaning any thing which falls within chapter 97' — no per-item threshold stated, unlike the £250 floor for carpets, clothing, watches, tableware, sports goods (paras 22–23) or £42,000 for vehicles (para 18). Paragraph 11 lists jewellery, precious metals and stones by commodity code without a price threshold. Later amendments: S.I. 2023/1364, S.I. 2025/504, S.I. 2026/543.
walls.authority: UK Parliament / Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office; enforced by HMRC and OFSI. The regulation number that prohibits export of Schedule 3A goods was not on the opened page.

walls.n: US and G7: luxury-goods ban including art and antiques (March 2022); OFAC designations and KleptoCapture enforcement
walls.cite: Announced 15 March 2022 by the UK with its G7 allies; The Art Newspaper (31 Mar 2022) names OFAC, the European Commission and OFSI as the enforcing bodies, notes that selling art to a non-designated Russian individual stays legal while any dealing with a designated person or entity risks fines or prison, and that freeports in New York, Geneva and Luxembourg were not then restricted. The US executive order and Commerce rule numbers were not opened and are not cited here. Enforcement record: Bonham-Carter indictment (October 2022, three sanctions-conspiracy counts, one IEEPA count, one wire-fraud count, 20 years maximum each); New York federal subpoenas to auction houses (February 2023); Senate PSI recommendation (July 2020) to bring high-value art under the Bank Secrecy Act.
walls.authority: US Treasury OFAC; US Department of Justice (Southern District of New York); US Senate PSI

walls.n: Russia: cultural-property export licence and permit (Law 4804-1)
walls.cite: Law of the Russian Federation No. 4804-1 of 15 April 1993 'О вывозе и ввозе культурных ценностей', as amended by Federal Law No. 435-FZ of 28 December 2017 and later acts (edition of 31 July 2025 shown): Article 5 (definitions), Article 35.1 (cultural valuables not exportable without an obligation of re-import), Article 35.2 (export), Article 35.3 (procedure for issuing to individuals a conclusion/permit — 'заключение (разрешительный документ)' — for export of cultural valuables for personal use), Article 35.4 (obtaining an export licence); Article 35.11 ceased to apply on 1 January 2024 under Federal Law No. 327-FZ of 24 July 2023. The Ministry of Culture's information note on 435-FZ states that individuals exporting cultural valuables for personal use must obtain a Ministry permit ('необходимо получить соответствующее разрешение Минкультуры России'), that permanent export of 'культурные ценности, имеющие особое значение' is banned, that movement within the EAEU is governed by EAEU law, that expert examination of imported valuables is voluntary and that insurance is mandatory for temporary export of state and municipal museum and archive holdings. The 50-year and 100-year age criteria that sort items between free export, permit and licence were not read in the statute text (article pages not opened) and are left in 'unconfirmed'.
walls.authority: Ministry of Culture of the Russian Federation (licences and permits); EAEU law for intra-union movement; customs (FCS) at the border
src: zakonrf.info, Law 4804-1 (ред. от 31.07.2025), table of contents

walls.n: Russia: Bank of Russia limits on taking money out
walls.cite: Bank of Russia decision of 26 September 2025, in force 1 October 2025 to 31 March 2026: Russian residents and non-residents from friendly countries may transfer up to US$1m a month (or equivalent) to foreign bank accounts and up to US$10,000 a month through money-transfer systems; the ban on transfers abroad continues for non-residents from unfriendly countries who do not work in Russia and for legal entities from those states; non-resident employees may remit wages. These caps bound what a Russian buyer can pay a foreign auction house or dealer from Russia. The cash-currency export limit was not on the opened page.
walls.authority: Central Bank of the Russian Federation
src: Bank of Russia press release, 26 Sep 2025

walls.cite: Full ban on direct EU imports of non-industrial diamonds and diamond jewellery from Russia from January 2024; partial embargo on Russian diamonds processed in third countries from 1 March 2024; full ban from 1 September 2024 (as summarised by bne IntelliNews; the regulation text was not opened).
